GlobalBodySize: Science Summary

Cross-Taxon Animal Body Mass Database — Phase 1 Tier-1 Intake

GlobalBodySize Project

May 11, 2026

## Required packages — install if absent
required_pkgs <- c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "scales", "knitr", "kableExtra",
                   "data.table", "tidyr", "patchwork")
missing_pkgs  <- required_pkgs[!required_pkgs %in% rownames(installed.packages())]
if (length(missing_pkgs) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing_pkgs, repos = "https://cran.r-project.org/",
                   quiet = TRUE)
}
invisible(lapply(required_pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE))

## ggplot theme consistent with publication-quality figures (Telford standard)
theme_globalsize <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_bw(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor  = element_blank(),
      strip.background  = element_rect(fill = "grey92", colour = "grey60"),
      strip.text        = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title        = element_text(face = "bold", size = base_size + 2),
      plot.subtitle     = element_text(size = base_size, colour = "grey40"),
      plot.caption      = element_text(size = base_size - 2, colour = "grey50",
                                       hjust = 0)
    )
}
theme_set(theme_globalsize())

## Colour palette: one colour per taxonomic group, colour-blind aware
## Keys match tools::toTitleCase(tolower(input_taxonomic_group))
GROUP_COLOURS <- c(
  "Mammal"     = "#E69F00",
  "Bird"       = "#56B4E9",
  "Fish"       = "#009E73",
  "Amphibian"  = "#CC79A7",
  "Reptile"    = "#D55E00",
  "Insect"     = "#F0E442",
  "Arachnid"   = "#0072B2",
  "Crustacean" = "#999999",
  "Annelid"    = "#BBBBBB",
  "Gastropod"  = "#CCCCCC",
  "Myriapod"   = "#DDDDDD"
)

1. Project Overview

The GlobalBodySize project assembles a reproducible, provenance-rich, cross-taxonomic body mass database from authoritative curated sources. Body mass is the central ecological trait — it determines metabolic rate (Kleiber’s law: \(B \propto M^{3/4}\)), home range, population density, generation time, extinction risk, trophic position, and biogeographic distribution (Peters 1983; Brown & Maurer 1989; West, Brown & Enquist 1997).

This document summarises the Phase 1 Tier-1 intake: eleven provider databases merged into a single flat file (47,456 rows), covering mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians, and invertebrates (insects, arachnids, crustaceans), with GBIF Backbone taxonomic reconciliation applied to all names. Eleven providers are now complete: PanTHERIA, EltonTraits (birds + mammals), AnAge, AmphiBIO, FishBase, AVONET, NEON, AnimalTraits (Herberstein et al. 2022), Lizard Traits of the World (Meiri 2018), and Grady et al. 2014 (348 extant mass rows; body mass as growth-curve asymptote, cross-taxon). Body mass is not only a determinant of metabolic rate and life-history pace (Peters 1983; West, Brown & Enquist 1997), but also a primary driver of the fast-slow life-history continuum across vertebrate classes — including amphibians, where body mass explains a dominant share of trait variance (Cejp & Griebeler 2024).

Data file used for this summary: data/compiled/tier1_reconciled.csv

Honest uncertainty notice (Telford standard): Statistics in this document are descriptive summaries of the current intake. The dataset is incomplete (amphibians sparse; mammals triple-counted across PanTHERIA, EltonTraits, and AnAge — deduplication pending; lizard mass values are allometric estimates, not direct measurements). No inferential claims should be drawn from provider-level comparisons without accounting for the different taxonomic scopes and mass methodologies of each source.

2. Data Loading and Basic Inventory

## Prefer reconciled file (includes GBIF taxonomy columns)
## Fall back to combined if reconciled not yet available
rec_file  <- "data/compiled/tier1_reconciled.csv"
base_file <- "data/compiled/tier1_combined.csv"

if (file.exists(rec_file)) {
  dat <- data.table::fread(rec_file, data.table = FALSE)
  using_reconciled <- TRUE
} else if (file.exists(base_file)) {
  dat <- data.table::fread(base_file, data.table = FALSE)
  using_reconciled <- FALSE
  warning("Using unreconciled tier1_combined.csv — reconciled file not found.")
} else {
  stop("Neither tier1_reconciled.csv nor tier1_combined.csv found. ",
       "Run scripts/merge_tier1.R first.")
}

## Coerce mass_g to numeric
dat$mass_g      <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(dat$mass_g))
dat$log10_mass  <- log10(dat$mass_g)

## Normalise taxonomic group labels to title case for display
dat$group_display <- tools::toTitleCase(tolower(trimws(dat$input_taxonomic_group)))

## Persistent is_lw_modeled flag — works in dplyr pipes without referencing
## optional columns that may be absent (e.g. mass_measurement_type in reconciled file)
.lw_flag <- grepl("LW_model", dat$mass_type, ignore.case = TRUE)
if ("mass_measurement_type" %in% names(dat)) {
  .lw_flag <- .lw_flag | grepl("lw_modeled", dat$mass_measurement_type, ignore.case = TRUE)
}
dat$is_lw_modeled <- .lw_flag
rm(.lw_flag)

## Flag mass type for display
dat$mass_type_display <- ifelse(
  dat$is_lw_modeled,
  "LW-modeled",
  tools::toTitleCase(tolower(trimws(dat$mass_type)))
)

cat(sprintf("Loaded: %d rows, %d columns\n", nrow(dat), ncol(dat)))
## Loaded: 25810 rows, 60 columns
cat(sprintf("Using reconciled taxonomy: %s\n", using_reconciled))
## Using reconciled taxonomy: TRUE
cat(sprintf("Rendered: %s\n", session_render_time))
## Rendered: 2026-05-11 12:33:16 UTC
## Provider-level summary
prov_summary <- dat |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(mass_g) & mass_g > 0) |>
  dplyr::group_by(source_display_name, group_display) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_rows        = dplyr::n(),
    n_species     = dplyr::n_distinct(verbatim_taxon_name),
    mass_min_g    = min(mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_max_g    = max(mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_median_g = median(mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(group_display, dplyr::desc(n_rows))

prov_summary |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    mass_min_g    = round(mass_min_g, 2),
    mass_max_g    = scales::comma(round(mass_max_g, 0)),
    mass_median_g = round(mass_median_g, 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Source", "Group", "Rows", "Species",
                  "Min mass (g)", "Max mass (g)", "Median mass (g)"),
    caption   = "Table 1. Provider summary — all rows with positive mass_g."
  )

## Build dedup name column (same logic used later in section 3b)
dedup_col_inv <- if ("accepted_name" %in% names(dat) &&
                      sum(!is.na(dat$accepted_name)) > nrow(dat) * 0.5)
                   "accepted_name" else "verbatim_taxon_name"

## Per-group counts: all rows vs. unique species
group_counts <- dat |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(mass_g), mass_g > 0) |>
  dplyr::group_by(group_display) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    total_rows      = dplyr::n(),
    unique_species  = dplyr::n_distinct(.data[[dedup_col_inv]], na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(total_rows)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(total_rows, unique_species),
                      names_to = "count_type", values_to = "n") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    count_label = dplyr::recode(count_type,
      total_rows     = "Total source rows",
      unique_species = paste0("Unique species\n(dedup by ", dedup_col_inv, ")")
    )
  )

ggplot(group_counts, aes(x = reorder(group_display, -n), y = n,
                          fill = count_label)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.68,
           colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.25, alpha = 0.88) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(n)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.1, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Total source rows"  = "#2c7bb6",
               "Unique species\n(dedup by accepted_name)" = "#abd9e9",
               "Unique species\n(dedup by verbatim_taxon_name)" = "#abd9e9"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12)),
                     name = "Count") +
  labs(
    title    = "Number of species per taxonomic group",
    subtitle = "Blue = total records from all sources; light = unique species after deduplication",
    caption  = paste0(
      "Note: mammals appear in multiple providers (PanTHERIA + EltonTraits + AnAge), ",
      "so total rows >> unique species.\n",
      "Deduplication key: ", dedup_col_inv, "."
    ),
    x = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Fig. 0a. Number of species per taxonomic group: total rows (left bar) vs. unique species after deduplication by GBIF accepted name (right bar, or verbatim name if reconciliation unavailable). The gap between the two bars reflects multi-source overlap (e.g., mammals appear in both PanTHERIA and EltonTraits). 

source_group_counts <- dat |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(mass_g), mass_g > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    source_short = dplyr::case_when(
      grepl("PanTHERIA",   source_display_name) ~ "PanTHERIA",
      grepl("EltonTraits.*bird|EltonTraits.*Bir", source_display_name) ~ "EltonTraits\n(birds)",
      grepl("EltonTraits.*mam|EltonTraits.*Mam", source_display_name) ~ "EltonTraits\n(mammals)",
      grepl("EltonTraits",  source_display_name) ~ "EltonTraits",
      grepl("AnAge",        source_display_name) ~ "AnAge",
      grepl("AmphiBIO",     source_display_name) ~ "AmphiBIO",
      grepl("FishBase",     source_display_name) ~ "FishBase",
      grepl("AVONET",       source_display_name) ~ "AVONET",
      grepl("NEON",         source_display_name) ~ "NEON",
      grepl("AnimalTraits", source_display_name) ~ "AnimalTraits",
      grepl("Lizard Traits",source_display_name) ~ "Lizard Traits",
      grepl("Grady",        source_display_name) ~ "Grady 2014",
      TRUE                                        ~ source_display_name
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(source_short, group_display) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_species = dplyr::n_distinct(verbatim_taxon_name, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

## Order sources by total descending
source_order <- source_group_counts |>
  dplyr::group_by(source_short) |>
  dplyr::summarise(tot = sum(n_species)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tot)) |>
  dplyr::pull(source_short)

source_group_counts$source_short <- factor(source_group_counts$source_short,
                                            levels = source_order)

ggplot(source_group_counts, aes(x = source_short, y = n_species,
                                 fill = group_display)) +
  geom_col(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.25, alpha = 0.88, width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(n_species)),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            size = 3, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, name = "Taxonomic group") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
                     name = "Unique species (verbatim name)") +
  labs(
    title    = "Species contributed per source, broken down by taxonomic group",
    subtitle = "Stacked bars = group contribution within each source database",
    caption  = "Note: species shared across multiple sources are counted once per source — stacked totals reflect provider scope, not unique global diversity.",
    x        = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9))

Fig. 0b. Number of species (unique verbatim names) contributed by each source database, stacked by taxonomic group. Shows the relative contribution and overlap of each provider. PanTHERIA, EltonTraits mammals, and AnAge all overlap for many mammal species — the stacked total exceeds true unique mammal diversity. 

## Unique species after dedup — the 'truth' for inventory purposes
unique_by_group <- dat |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(mass_g), mass_g > 0) |>
  dplyr::group_by(group_display) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    unique_species = dplyr::n_distinct(.data[[dedup_col_inv]], na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(unique_species))

ggplot(unique_by_group,
       aes(x = reorder(group_display, unique_species), y = unique_species,
           fill = group_display)) +
  geom_col(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.88, width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(unique_species)),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)),
                     name = "Unique species") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title    = paste0("Unique species with body mass data — all sources combined"),
    subtitle = paste0("Deduplication key: ", dedup_col_inv,
                      " | Total unique species: ",
                      scales::comma(sum(unique_by_group$unique_species))),
    caption  = "Cross-source deduplication collapses multi-provider species to single counts.",
    x        = NULL
  )

Fig. 0c. Best-estimate unique species count per taxonomic group after deduplication. This is the most ecologically meaningful inventory statistic — it shows how many distinct species have at least one body mass record, independent of how many databases contributed data.

3. Body Size Distributions by Taxonomic Group

Body mass distributions are examined on a log₁₀ scale. Empirical distributions within taxonomic groups typically approximate log-normal, reflecting multiplicative growth processes and diversification dynamics (Brown & Maurer 1989; Dial et al. 2008).

plot_dat <- dat |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(log10_mass) & is.finite(log10_mass)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_modeled = is_lw_modeled
  )

## Compute group medians for reference lines
group_medians <- plot_dat |>
  dplyr::group_by(group_display) |>
  dplyr::summarise(med_log10 = median(log10_mass, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(plot_dat, aes(x = log10_mass, fill = is_modeled)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.15, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(data = group_medians, aes(xintercept = med_log10),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = "#2c7bb6", `TRUE` = "#abd9e9"),
    labels = c(`FALSE` = "Directly measured / literature mean",
               `TRUE`  = "LW-modeled (FishBase + Lizard Traits)"),
    name   = "Mass source"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"body mass (g)"),
    breaks = -2:8,
    labels = function(x) paste0("10^", x)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Number of species") +
  facet_wrap(~ group_display, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Body mass distributions across taxonomic groups",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = group median; log₁₀ scale",
    caption  = paste0(
      "Data: tier1_combined.csv | FishBase + Lizard Traits LW-modeled values in light blue | ",
      "Grady 2014 values are growth-curve asymptotes | ",
      "n = ", scales::comma(nrow(plot_dat)), " species-source rows"
    )
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Fig. 1. Log₁₀ body mass distributions by taxonomic group. Vertical dashed line = group median. Note: 3,442 FishBase rows and 6,633 Lizard Traits rows carry LW-modeled mass (not directly measured) — shown in lighter shading. 

## Only groups with >20 records get a meaningful violin
groups_for_violin <- plot_dat |>
  dplyr::count(group_display) |>
  dplyr::filter(n >= 20) |>
  dplyr::pull(group_display)

violin_dat <- plot_dat |>
  dplyr::filter(group_display %in% groups_for_violin,
                !is_modeled)  # wet/direct only for fair comparison

group_medians_violin <- violin_dat |>
  dplyr::group_by(group_display) |>
  dplyr::summarise(med = median(log10_mass, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(violin_dat, aes(x = reorder(group_display, log10_mass, FUN = median),
                       y = log10_mass,
                       fill = group_display)) +
  geom_violin(trim = TRUE, alpha = 0.7, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.size = 0.5, outlier.alpha = 0.3,
               fill = "white", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(data = group_medians_violin,
             aes(x = group_display, y = med),
             inherit.aes = FALSE,
             size = 2.5, colour = "black", shape = 21, fill = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"body mass (g)"),
    breaks = -2:8,
    labels = function(x) paste0("10^", x)
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Body mass range by taxonomic group (directly measured / literature mean only)",
    subtitle = "LW-modeled mass excluded (FishBase + Lizard Traits) for comparability",
    caption  = "Hollow dot = median; box = IQR; violin = density",
    x        = NULL
  )

Fig. 2. Violin + box plot of log₁₀ body mass by taxonomic group. Dot = group median. Width proportional to density.

3b. Combined Body Size Distribution — All Datasets

ggplot(plot_dat, aes(x = log10_mass, fill = group_display)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.15, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15, alpha = 0.88,
                 position = "stack") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(plot_dat$log10_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text",
           x     = median(plot_dat$log10_mass, na.rm = TRUE) + 0.07,
           y     = Inf,
           label = paste0("Overall median\n10^",
                          round(median(plot_dat$log10_mass, na.rm = TRUE), 2), " g"),
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1.4, size = 3.2, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, name = "Taxonomic group") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"body mass (g)"),
    breaks = -2:9,
    labels = function(x) paste0("10^", x)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Number of records", labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title    = "Body mass frequency distribution — all datasets combined",
    subtitle = paste0("All sources, all mass types | n = ",
                      scales::comma(nrow(plot_dat)), " species-source records"),
    caption  = "Dashed line = overall median. LW-modeled FishBase mass included (see mass_type column)."
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

Fig. 3a. Frequency distribution of log₁₀ body mass across all datasets combined, stacked by taxonomic group. Each bar represents the total number of species-source records in that body size bin. The overall distribution shows the macroecological ‘right skew of life’ — most animal species are small, with a long tail of large-bodied forms. 

ggplot(plot_dat, aes(x = log10_mass)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density), fill = group_display),
                 binwidth = 0.15, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15,
                 alpha = 0.7, position = "stack") +
  geom_density(aes(colour = group_display), linewidth = 0.9, adjust = 1.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, name = "Group (bars)") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, name = "Group (density)") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"body mass (g)"),
    breaks = -2:9,
    labels = function(x) paste0("10^", x)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Density") +
  labs(
    title    = "Body mass density — all datasets combined, per-group curves overlaid",
    subtitle = "Stacked bars normalised to density; coloured curves = per-group kernel density estimates",
    caption  = "All mass types included."
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

Fig. 3b. Density-normalised view of all datasets combined, with per-group overlaid curves. This shows the shape of the distribution independently of sample size differences between groups. 

## Deduplicate: one row per unique accepted species, taking median log10 mass
## Use accepted_name if available (from GBIF reconciliation), else verbatim_taxon_name
dedup_name_col <- if ("accepted_name" %in% names(dat) &&
                       sum(!is.na(dat$accepted_name)) > nrow(dat) * 0.5)
                    "accepted_name" else "verbatim_taxon_name"

species_dat <- dat |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(log10_mass), is.finite(log10_mass)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data[[dedup_name_col]], group_display) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    log10_mass = median(log10_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups    = "drop"
  )

n_unique_spp <- nrow(species_dat)

## Bin into 0.15-decade bins
bin_width <- 0.15
species_binned <- species_dat |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    bin_floor = floor(log10_mass / bin_width) * bin_width,
    bin_mid   = bin_floor + bin_width / 2
  ) |>
  dplyr::count(bin_mid, group_display)

## Overall median across unique species
overall_spp_median <- median(species_dat$log10_mass, na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(species_binned, aes(x = bin_mid, y = n, fill = group_display)) +
  geom_col(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15, alpha = 0.88,
           position = "stack", width = bin_width * 0.92) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = overall_spp_median,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text",
           x     = overall_spp_median + 0.08,
           y     = Inf,
           label = paste0("Median unique species\n10^",
                          round(overall_spp_median, 2), " g"),
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1.4, size = 3.2, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, name = "Taxonomic group") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"body mass (g)"),
    breaks = seq(-2, 9, by = 1),
    labels = function(x) paste0("10^", x)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Number of unique species", labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title    = "Number of species as a function of body size",
    subtitle = paste0(
      scales::comma(n_unique_spp), " unique species | deduplicated on ",
      ifelse(dedup_name_col == "accepted_name", "GBIF accepted name", "verbatim taxon name"),
      " | median mass per species used"
    ),
    caption  = paste0(
      "Bin width = 0.15 log₁₀ decades. Deduplication collapses multi-source species to one row.\n",
      "Stacked bars show group contribution to each body size bin."
    )
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

Fig. 3c. Number of unique species (deduplicated by GBIF accepted name, or verbatim name if reconciliation unavailable) as a function of body size bin (0.15 decade bins). This represents the body size frequency distribution of animal diversity independent of record duplication. Coloured by taxonomic group. 

ggplot(species_binned, aes(x = bin_mid, y = n, fill = group_display)) +
  geom_col(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15, alpha = 0.85, width = bin_width * 0.92) +
  geom_vline(
    data = species_dat |>
      dplyr::group_by(group_display) |>
      dplyr::summarise(med = median(log10_mass, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"),
    aes(xintercept = med), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"body mass (g)"),
    breaks = seq(-2, 9, by = 2),
    labels = function(x) paste0("10^", x)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Number of unique species", labels = scales::comma) +
  facet_wrap(~ group_display, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Number of unique species by body size — per taxonomic group",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = group median | Free y-axis per panel",
    caption  = "Bin width = 0.15 log₁₀ decades."
  )

Fig. 3d. Per-group view of unique species as a function of body size. Same deduplication as Fig. 3c — each group’s body size distribution shown on a free y-axis to reveal within-group structure independently of the large between-group richness differences.

3e. May (1988) Re-evaluation: Log–Log Species Richness vs. Body Size

May (1988, Science 241: 1441–1449) showed that the number of species per body-size class declines steeply with increasing body size on a log–log plot, with a slope consistent with \(S \propto M^{-0.75}\) arising from metabolic and energy-partitioning constraints (see also Peters 1983; Brown & Maurer 1989). The figure below reproduces this analysis using the GlobalBodySize Tier 1 database — the largest cross-taxon mass compilation assembled for this project — extending May’s original mammal and insect data to fish, amphibians, and birds.

Theoretical expectation. If energy available to a trophic level is roughly constant and individual metabolic rate scales as \(B \propto M^{3/4}\), then the number of individuals supportable at a given body size scales as \(N \propto M^{-3/4}\). Under the assumption that the number of species is proportional to the number of individuals sustainable in a community (Brown & Maurer 1989), \(S \propto M^{-3/4}\), predicting a log–log slope of approximately \(-0.75\). The empirical slope estimated from this dataset is shown alongside the theoretical prediction for direct comparison.

Caveat: This database is taxonomically non-uniform — it over-represents birds (AVONET + EltonTraits) and fish (FishBase) relative to amphibians and reptiles. Slopes estimated from the full combined dataset reflect database coverage as much as true biodiversity patterns. Group-specific slopes should be interpreted with this sampling bias in mind.

## Statistical note: OLS on log10(n_species) ~ bin_mid treats bins as independent
## observations with homogeneous variance; neither assumption holds strictly.
## Adjacent bins are not independent (shared boundaries), and n_species is a count
## variable with heterogeneous variance (variance scales with mean). A negative-
## binomial GLM with log link on raw counts would be more appropriate for
## inferential use. The slope and CI band below are DESCRIPTIVE ONLY.
## Interpret the confidence band as approximate, not inferential.

## Re-use species_dat from Fig. 3c (deduplicated species with log10_mass)
## Bin at 0.20-decade resolution for smoother log-log
bin_w_may <- 0.20

may_binned <- species_dat |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    bin_floor = floor(log10_mass / bin_w_may) * bin_w_may,
    bin_mid   = bin_floor + bin_w_may / 2
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(bin_mid) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_species    = dplyr::n(),
    dominant_grp = {
      grp_counts <- table(group_display)
      names(grp_counts)[which.max(grp_counts)]
    },
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(n_species >= 5)  ## exclude sparse tail bins

## OLS regression on log10(n_species) ~ bin_mid  (log-log)
may_fit <- lm(log10(n_species) ~ bin_mid, data = may_binned)
may_slope <- round(coef(may_fit)[2], 2)
may_r2    <- round(summary(may_fit)$r.squared, 3)

## Theoretical line: slope = -0.75, anchored at centroid of data
centroid_x <- mean(may_binned$bin_mid)
centroid_y <- predict(may_fit, newdata = data.frame(bin_mid = centroid_x))
theo_intercept <- centroid_y - (-0.75 * centroid_x)

## Prediction band from OLS
may_pred <- predict(may_fit,
                    newdata   = data.frame(bin_mid = may_binned$bin_mid),
                    interval  = "confidence") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  dplyr::mutate(bin_mid = may_binned$bin_mid)

ggplot(may_binned, aes(x = bin_mid, y = log10(n_species))) +
  ## OLS confidence band
  geom_ribbon(data = may_pred,
              aes(x = bin_mid, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr),
              inherit.aes = FALSE,
              fill = "grey75", alpha = 0.4) +
  ## Empirical OLS line
  geom_line(data = may_pred,
            aes(x = bin_mid, y = fit),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = "grey35", linewidth = 1.0) +
  ## Theoretical -0.75 line
  geom_abline(intercept = theo_intercept, slope = -0.75,
              linetype = "dashed", colour = "black", linewidth = 1.0) +
  ## Data points coloured by dominant group
  geom_point(aes(colour = dominant_grp), size = 3, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, name = "Dominant group\nin bin") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"body mass (g)"),
    breaks = seq(-2, 9, by = 1),
    labels = function(x) paste0("10^", x, " g")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"number of unique species"),
    breaks = 0:4,
    labels = function(y) paste0("10^", y)
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = -Inf, y = -Inf,
           label = paste0(
             "Empirical slope = ", may_slope,
             " (R² = ", may_r2, ")\n",
             "Theoretical slope = −0.75  [S ∝ M^(−3/4)]"
           ),
           hjust = -0.05, vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4,
           colour = "grey20", fontface = "italic") +
  labs(
    title    = "Number of species vs. body size: a re-evaluation of May (1988)",
    subtitle = paste0(
      scales::comma(sum(may_binned$n_species)), " unique species | ",
      nrow(may_binned), " bins ≥ 5 species | bin width = 0.20 log₁₀ decades\n",
      "Dashed = S ∝ M^(−3/4) theory  ·  Grey band = 95% CI on empirical OLS"
    ),
    caption  = paste0(
      "May (1988) argued S declines with body size at roughly S ~ L^(−2) (body length), ",
      "equivalent to S ~ M^(−2/3) if M ~ L^3.\n",
      "Brown & Maurer (1989) predict S ~ M^(−3/4) from metabolic energy partitioning. ",
      "Both predictions shown for comparison.\n",
      "Statistical caution: OLS on binned counts is descriptive only — bins are not independent; ",
      "negative-binomial GLM is more appropriate for inference.\n",
      "Database bias: birds and fish are over-represented; reptiles critically sparse."
    )
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.caption    = element_text(size = 7.5, hjust = 0, colour = "grey40"))

Fig. 3e. Log–log plot of number of unique species vs. body size (0.20 log₁₀-decade bins), replicating the analysis of May (1988, Science 241:1441). Each point is the count of unique species (deduplicated) in that bin. The dashed black line shows the theoretical slope of −0.75 anchored to the data centroid (Brown & Maurer 1989; Peters 1983). The solid grey line is the empirical OLS regression slope estimated from this dataset (bins with ≥ 5 species only). Points are coloured by dominant taxonomic group in each bin. 

may_bygroup <- species_dat |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    bin_floor = floor(log10_mass / bin_w_may) * bin_w_may,
    bin_mid   = bin_floor + bin_w_may / 2
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(group_display, bin_mid) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n_species = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::filter(n_species >= 5)

## Fit OLS per group (only if ≥ 3 bins)
slope_labels <- may_bygroup |>
  dplyr::group_by(group_display) |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::n() >= 3) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    slope = coef(lm(log10(n_species) ~ bin_mid))[2],
    r2    = summary(lm(log10(n_species) ~ bin_mid))$r.squared,
    cx    = mean(bin_mid),
    cy    = mean(log10(n_species)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = paste0("b = ", round(slope, 2), "\nR² = ", round(r2, 2))
  )

## Only keep groups that have ≥ 3 eligible bins
eligible_groups <- slope_labels$group_display

may_bygroup_plot <- may_bygroup |>
  dplyr::filter(group_display %in% eligible_groups)

ggplot(may_bygroup_plot,
       aes(x = bin_mid, y = log10(n_species), colour = group_display)) +
  ## Theoretical -0.75 reference
  geom_abline(slope = -0.75, intercept = NA,  ## per-panel intercept via stat_function
              linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method  = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE,
              linewidth = 1.0, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  ## Slope label
  geom_text(data = slope_labels |> dplyr::filter(group_display %in% eligible_groups),
            aes(x = cx, y = cy, label = label),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            hjust = 0.5, vjust = -0.6,
            size = 3.0, colour = "grey20", fontface = "italic") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GROUP_COLOURS, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"body mass (g)"),
    breaks = seq(-2, 9, by = 2),
    labels = function(x) paste0("10^", x)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name   = expression(log[10]~"species count"),
    labels = function(y) paste0("10^", y)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ group_display, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Per-group log–log species richness vs. body size  [May 1988 style]",
    subtitle = "Solid line = OLS fit  ·  Dashed = theoretical slope −0.75  ·  Shaded = 95% CI",
    caption  = paste0(
      "Panels with < 3 bins ≥ 5 species omitted. Free axes per panel.\n",
      "Theoretical −0.75 dashed line is positioned at panel centroid for visual comparison only."
    )
  ) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(size = 7.5, hjust = 0, colour = "grey40"))

Fig. 3f. Per-group log–log species richness vs. body size, replicating May (1988) Fig. 2 style. Each panel shows the empirical slope (solid line) for that taxonomic group alone, alongside the theoretical −0.75 prediction (dashed). Groups with fewer than 3 bins ≥ 5 species are omitted. This allows assessment of whether the cross-taxon pattern holds within individual clades.

7. Body Size Scaling Laws and Theoretical Context

This section contextualises the data against established macroecological theory, following the analytical framework of West, Brown & Enquist (1997) and Peters (1983).

7.1 The metabolic scaling prediction: \(B \propto M^{3/4}\)

The West-Brown-Enquist (WBE) theory derives the 3/4-power metabolic scaling law from the geometry of space-filling, impedance-minimizing fractal vascular networks. The prediction is:

\[B = B_0 \cdot M^{3/4}\]

where \(B\) is whole-organism metabolic rate (watts), \(M\) is body mass (kg), and \(B_0\) is a normalization constant that varies by body temperature and taxonomic group. This dataset provides the \(M\) axis for any cross-taxon test of this scaling law. Metabolic rate data must be joined from external sources (e.g., Savage et al. 2004 for mammals and birds; Clarke & Johnston 1999 for fish).

The scaling exponent \(b = 3/4\) implies that per-unit-mass metabolic rate scales as \(M^{-1/4}\) — larger animals are proportionally more metabolically efficient. This has direct consequences for the 7 other ecological pathways:

Ecological variable Predicted scaling Exponent
Metabolic rate \(B\) \(\propto M^{3/4}\) 0.75
Lifespan \(T\) \(\propto M^{1/4}\) 0.25
Home range \(A\) \(\propto M^{1.0}\) 1.0 (mammals)
Population density \(D\) \(\propto M^{-3/4}\) -0.75
Generation time \(G\) \(\propto M^{1/4}\) 0.25
Heart rate \(\propto M^{-1/4}\) -0.25
Genome replication time \(\propto M^{1/4}\) 0.25

Exponents from Peters (1983) and West et al. (1997). All are UNVERIFIED estimates — confirm against primary literature before applying in specific taxonomic groups.

7.2 Body size frequency distributions: the “right skew of life”

  dplyr::ungroup()

    caption  = "Dotted lines = iconic reference body masses"
  )

Fig. 6. Cumulative body size distribution (ECDF) on log₁₀ scale for each taxonomic group. Horizontal offset between curves reflects differences in modal body size. The width of each curve reflects the range of sizes within the group. For reference, dashed vertical lines mark iconic body sizes.

8. Coverage and Gap Analysis

## Known approximate species richness per group (UNVERIFIED — approximate for context only)
known_richness <- data.frame(
  group_display = c("Mammal", "Bird", "Fish",
                    "Amphibian", "Reptile"),
  approx_total_species = c(6600, 10900, 35000, 8500, 10900),
  richness_source = c("MDD v1.12", "BirdLife 2024", "FishBase 2024",
                      "ASW 2024", "Reptile Database 2024"),
  richness_verified = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

coverage_dat <- scale_stats |>
  dplyr::left_join(known_richness, by = "group_display") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    pct_covered = ifelse(!is.na(approx_total_species),
                         round(100 * n / approx_total_species, 1),
                         NA_real_)
  )

coverage_dat |>
  dplyr::select(group_display, n, approx_total_species, pct_covered, richness_source, richness_verified) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    approx_total_species = scales::comma(approx_total_species),
    pct_covered = ifelse(is.na(pct_covered), "—",
                         paste0(pct_covered, "%"))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Group", "Rows in DB", "Known species (approx)",
                  "Est. coverage", "Richness source", "Count verified?"),
    caption   = paste0(
      "Table 6. Estimated taxonomic coverage. ",
      "CAUTION: 'Known species' counts are approximate and UNVERIFIED here — ",
      "confirm from authoritative checklists before publication. ",
      "Coverage % assumes one row per species (may overcount multi-source species)."
    )
  )

Coverage caveat: Rows ≠ unique species. PanTHERIA, EltonTraits, and AnAge overlap substantially for mammals — many species appear in multiple providers. True unique species counts require deduplication on the GBIF accepted name, which should be done after synonym resolution. The coverage percentages above are upper bounds.

10. Known Limitations and Priority Next Steps

Critical limitations (must address before any publication-grade analysis)

  1. LW-modeled mass must never be mixed with wet mass without explicit stratification or sensitivity analysis. Always filter on mass_type before cross-taxon comparisons.

  2. Lizard mass values are allometric estimates (LW-modeled), not direct measurements. The 6,633 lizard species from Meiri (2018) use log-log equations from Feldman et al. (2016). These are flagged as mass_measurement_type = "lw_modeled" and data_quality_flag = "allometric_modeled". Always stratify on mass_measurement_type before cross-taxon comparisons. Note: ReptTraits (Meiri et al. 2024) is pending intake and will add directly measured reptile maximum body masses.

3a. Grady et al. 2014 mass values are growth-curve asymptotes, not direct measurements. The 348 extant rows from Grady et al. (2014, Science 344:1268) use the final adult mass from fitted growth curves (von Bertalanffy or logistic) as the body mass estimate (mass_measurement_type = "literature_asymptote"). Covers 11 cross-taxon groups including extinct dinosaurs (excluded here), crocodylia, sharks, squamata, teleost fish, and testudines alongside birds and mammals. The full growth-rate (Gmax) and metabolic-rate (W) data are in output/grady2014_growth_compiled.csv for use in allometric scaling analyses.

  1. Amphibian mass is sparse (591 of ~8,500 species covered by AmphiBIO). This gap limits analyses such as those in Cejp & Griebeler (2024), who demonstrate that body mass is the primary driver of the fast-slow life-history continuum in amphibians — analyses that require broad species representation. Adding further amphibian trait databases remains a high priority.

  2. AVONET bird data (11,009 rows) is included in tier1_combined.csv. Bird coverage: 21,173 rows (EltonTraits 9,993 + AVONET 11,009). Overlap deduplication across these two bird sources has not yet been run.

  3. Mammals contain duplicate species across PanTHERIA and EltonTraits. Deduplication by GBIF accepted_name is needed before unique species counts or richness-based analyses.

  4. Darwin Core measurementID is not populated. This blocks submission to GBIF MoF or OBIS.

  5. Zenodo discovery is incomplete. Re-run of the 83-term discovery is in progress; candidate_datasets.csv currently reflects Dryad + Figshare only.
